tagline: A fogbound town where everyone stopped existing — and something stayed behind.

now.next: Safe-room warmth, fog as pressure, one deliberate encounter

bible.epigraph: Atmosphere before spectacle. Tension before power fantasy. The fog is not decoration — it is the world thinking.
bible.logline: Third-person survival horror in Unreal Engine: a coastal town emptied of people, thick with fog, where scarcity, sound, and what you cannot see matter more than what you can shoot.
bible.inspiration: Draws on the design philosophies of classic and modern survival horror — resource dread, oppressive place, psychological weather — while building its own setting, lore, mechanics, visual identity, and horror language.

priority.label: Atmosphere
priority.note: Place first. Mood is the product.

priority.label: Survival
priority.note: Scarcity makes every door a decision.

priority.label: Spectacle
priority.note: Earn it. Never lead with it.

fog.title: The Fog
fog.lede: Fog is part of Stillwater's identity. It should become more than a visual effect.
systems: Conceal enemies and soften distant silhouettes
Change visibility and make landmarks unreliable
Hide and reveal paths as weather shifts
Carry sound differently — muffled, close, wrong

audio.title: Audio as system
audio.lede: Treat sound as gameplay. The town should speak before it shows its teeth.
cues: Breathing and wind through empty streets
Rain on roofs, building creaks, settling timber
Distant machinery that may not be machinery

survival.title: Survival grammar
survival.lede: Classic usability with Stillwater weight — limited inventory, deliberate combat, rooms you are reluctant to leave.
tenets: Limited inventory: weapons, ammo, healing, keys, puzzle pieces
Safe rooms as emotional anchors — warmth against the fog
Encounters should feel costly and readable
Exploration loops beat constant forward pressure

bible.workingPrompt: Build Stillwater as fogbound third-person survival horror: emptied town, oppressive weather, scarce resources, audio-as-threat, safe rooms that feel like mercy. Prioritize atmosphere, tension, exploration, then survival; spectacle last. Every feature must deepen place, dread, or meaningful choice — never power fantasy for its own sake.
